One evening in 1949, while | was still serving in Congress, | received an anonymous call at my home. A male voice said three words, "Watch Jeane Dixon," and hung up the telephone.

A week later, the psychic Jeane Dixon held a press conference. One of the reporters asked her to predict my future. She drew a blank, however, explaining that she needed time to meditate. | believe that in show business parlance this is known as "milking the audience." Finally she said it: "| predict that one day Richard Nixon will become president of the
United States."

| could only conclude that the higher source from which she had received her intelligence was not necessarily supernatural. When | lost the presidential election to John F. Kennedy in 1960, Jeane Dixon continued to predict that | would be president. "Destiny," she said, "cannot be

denied."
